extracted.intended_audience: classroom teachers, teacher-educators, and educational researchers interested in formative assessment
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical and practical guidance for designing and enacting formative assessment in classroom settings, including core strategies, models for interpreting student responses, and guidance on constructing feedback to improve learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative assessment definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice in a classroom is formative to the extent that evidence about student achievement is elicited, interpreted, and used by teachers, learners, or their peers, to make decisions about the next steps in instruction that are likely to be better, or better founded, than the decisions they would have taken in the absence of the evidence that was elicited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifications in the paper: 'instruction' is any activity intended to create learning; the focus is on decisions (not merely collecting evidence) — the evidence must be used to make decisions that are likely to be better or at least better founded; agents may be teacher, peer, or learner; the probabilistic phrasing recognises interventions may not always produce better learning in every case. Do not count evidence collection alone as formative; ensure evidence informs decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three processes in learning and teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing where the learners are in their learning; establishing where they are going; establishing what needs to be done to get them there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three processes (from Ramaprasad) form the analytic backbone for formative assessment design. Responsibility can be shared among teacher, peers and learners; crossing these processes with agents clarifies which actions enact formative assessment. Assessment tasks and feedback should address all three processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarifying and sharing learning intentions and criteria for success
rubrics_metrics.description: Make explicit learning intentions and success criteria to learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharing success criteria helps learners understand what is valued and supports self- and peer-assessment. The paper cites Clarke (2001) and emphasises that communicating criteria reduces misinterpretation of tasks and standards and supports interpretable student responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineering effective classroom discussions and tasks that elicit evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and orchestrate discussions and learning tasks specifically to elicit evidence of student understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes classroom questioning practices, design of tasks that produce interpretable responses, and attention to whole-class interaction dynamics. Beware the rote I-R-E pattern; aim for dialogic exchanges that reveal students' thinking. Use both synchronous (real-time discussion) and asynchronous (exit tickets, homework) elicitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing feedback that moves learners forward
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide feedback (from teachers, peers, or self) that helps learners take the next steps in learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feedback must be interpretive and actionable — it is formative only if the information is used to improve performance or to ground decisions. Feedback examples include comment-only marking. Feedback should aim to be 'likely' to improve decisions (probabilistic standard). Consider levels of feedback (task/process/self-regulation) and avoid feedback that only evaluates correctness without guiding next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activating students as instructional resources for one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Use peer-assessment and collaborative structures so students support each other's learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This involves reciprocal teaching, cooperative learning, and structuring interactions so students provide useful evidence and feedback for peers. Peer activity can enact formative strategies when students are trained in assessment criteria and discussion norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activating students as owners of their own learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop learners' capacity for self-assessment, metacognition, and volitional strategies so they regulate their own learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Links to self-regulated learning: support metacognitive monitoring, planning, and adapting; foster motivation and attributional styles that keep learners on a 'growth' track rather than a 'well-being' avoidance track. Make self-assessment overt and useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original classroom activities linked to formative assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Five practical activity types commonly used as formative practices: sharing success criteria with learners; classroom questioning; comment-only marking; peer- and self-assessment; formative use of summative tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These activities are pragmatic ways to enact the five key strategies. The paper notes risks of superficial adoption and emphasises linking each activity to the underlying rationale so practice is not a checklist but a coherent approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative use of summative tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Use summative tests formatively by eliciting evidence that informs next instructional steps and by communicating what is valued in the discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summative-style tests can, when used appropriately, provide evidence for feedback, communicate success criteria, enable peer help, and guide student revision planning. But tests designed primarily for summative purposes may not automatically serve formative ends unless repurposed and interpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moments of contingency
rubrics_metrics.description: Formative assessment focuses on creating and capitalizing upon 'moments of contingency' — instances where elicited evidence can change instructional decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These moments can be synchronous (real-time adjustments) or asynchronous (feedback that informs future lessons). Capitalising on such moments links assessment to instructional regulation. Teachers should look for and design opportunities that create contingency moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agents of assessment: teacher, peer, learner
rubrics_metrics.description: Formative assessment agents include teachers, learners themselves, and peers — each can elicit, interpret, and use evidence to make instructional decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interventions that distribute responsibility appropriately: teacher-led diagnosis, peer feedback mechanisms, and structures that enable learners to act on evidence. The paper stresses joint and several responsibility: both teachers and learners should mitigate the other's failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic and prognostic decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-step decision process in formative interaction: diagnostic (interpreting a student response to infer understanding) and prognostic (choosing the best instructional response).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers must rapidly interpret responses (interpretive listening) and then select a tactical response consistent with strategic goals. Both steps are complex and often time-pressured; training should support rapid, accurate diagnosis and appropriate prognoses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of listening and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Different teacher listening modes affect interpretation: 'evaluative listening' (focus on correctness), 'interpretive listening' (seek understanding of student thinking), and 'hermeneutic listening' (teacher's thinking modified by exchange).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective formative practice requires moving beyond evaluative listening toward interpretive/hermeneutic listening so responses reveal student reasoning. Avoid moves that only seek correct responses; invite explanation and elaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: I-R-E interaction quality (initiation-response-evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The common initiation-response-evaluation sequence can be either dialogic (revealing and productive) or a restrictive pattern that keeps students in a supporting role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design questioning and follow-up to avoid mere recall/fill-in behaviors (teacher 'Almost'/'Nearly') and instead promote genuine student thinking. Use follow-ups that solicit explanation, reasoning, and elaboration rather than simply judging correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider multiple possible causes of imperfect output
rubrics_metrics.description: When a student produces an imperfect response, teachers should consider a range of explanations (misunderstood language, misunderstood purpose, superficial errors, task misinterpretation, ineffective strategy, lack of criteria understanding, need for deeper explanation, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper lists explicit possible causes; teachers should diagnostically consider these before selecting feedback. Example cases illustrate how different diagnoses require different responses (e.g., invite explanation vs teach conceptual point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic versus tactical levels of feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish strategic decisions (guided by broader pedagogical orientation and learning aims) from tactical formulation (the fine-grain wording of the immediate response).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic level: what overall purpose is being pursued? Tactical level: how to phrase the next move to serve that strategy. Teachers should ensure tactical moves align with strategic aims and be aware that the same tactical move may be appropriate or not depending on strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design diagnostic questions for interpretability
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft diagnostic questions so student responses are interpretable and reveal underlying thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic questions should avoid ambiguous prompts whose responses are hard to interpret. The paper references work on analyzing diagnostic questions and stresses value even in single well-designed diagnostic items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-regulated learning model for mediating interpretation and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Use SRL frameworks (e.g., Winne & Hadwin): stages of identify task, plan response, enact strategy, adapt/review; and resources/conditions (A: conditions; B: operations; C: standards; D: evaluation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SRL models help teachers understand internal learner processes and thus inform diagnosis and feedback. Support students' standards for self-appraisal, volitional strategies, and metacognitive monitoring so feedback can engage these processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject- and context-sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Formative practices must respect subject-specific epistemologies, age differences, and classroom social norms; what counts as good explanation varies by subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid universal 'rules' for feedback; consider disciplinary norms (e.g., mathematics vs history), student developmental level, and local classroom norms when choosing feedback moves and designing tasks. The paper warns against transferring rules across subjects uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superficial adoption; require coherent theoretical grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not adopt formative practices superficially as isolated techniques; link practice to theoretical rationale and upstream planning to create a favourable context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper documents problems of superficial adoption and recommends connecting activities to theory (SRL, discourse) and providing teacher support (professional communities) to effect substantive change rather than checklist implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and modality of formative interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise both synchronous (real-time teacher moves, whole-class discussion) and asynchronous (written feedback, homework analysis, exit passes) modes of formative interaction and plan accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different modes afford different opportunities: synchronous moves permit immediate contingency and adaptation; asynchronous feedback can inform future lessons or students' revision. Use both and design tasks so asynchronous evidence is interpretable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of feedback, fine-grain and differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the level (task/process/self-regulation), the fine-grain of feedback wording, and differentiation across learners when designing formative feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper highlights 'levels of feedback, the fine-grain of feedback and differentiation' as key themes: feedback should be tailored to learner's current resources and understanding, differentiated for diverse needs, and formulated at the appropriate level to support next-step learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher builds models of pupil learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers should develop models of how pupils learn (their mental representations, strategies, and misconceptions) to craft feedback that is likely to be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional development should include psychology of learning; examples from the paper show teachers requesting training in learning theory to improve the predictive usefulness of their feedback. Models are necessary (though not sufficient) for valid diagnosis.
